chapter_note.about: Every programming question in GATE asks the same thing: what does this code do? This chapter rebuilds the seven pieces you need to answer it by hand: variables, integer division and modulo, if/else, loops, arrays, functions and nested loops. Each card shows the idea as a picture, and shows C and Python side by side wherever they differ. The method never changes: write the variables as boxes, go line by line, and keep a trace table. Slow and exact beats fast and guessed.
chapter_note.simple: A program is a list of instructions that the computer follows one at a time. To know what a program does, you act like the computer: write each variable in a box, do each line, and update the boxes. Loops repeat lines, if/else picks one path, and an array is a row of boxes numbered from 0. A function is a helper that works on copies of what you hand it. Division with leftovers (`//` and `%`) turns up everywhere. If you can do all this by hand with a small table, you can answer almost any output question.

gate_patterns: Output tracing in C and Python: a short program with loops, an array and a function call, and the question is 'what is printed?'. Foundation, used in: ds.c, ds.python, ds.recursion.
Counting how many times a statement runs (nested loops, steps like `i *= 2`) is the first step of complexity analysis. Foundation, used in: algo.complexity, algo.sorting, algo.searching.

cards.title: Variables and assignment
cards.simple: A variable is a labelled box that holds one value. Picture a locker with a name on the door: the name is `x` and the stuff inside is `5`. The line `y = x + 2` means: look inside locker x, add 2, and put the answer in locker y. If you later put something new into locker x, locker y does not care, because it already holds its own copy. Putting a new value into a box throws the old one away. In exam words: `=` is assignment, not equality. It works out the right side first and stores the result in the variable on the left.
cards.idea: A **variable** is a name for a box in memory that holds one value. The line `x = 5` puts 5 in box x. The right side is worked out first, using what the boxes hold right now, and then the answer goes into the box on the left. Whatever was in that box before is gone.
cards.definition:
`name = expression` evaluates the expression, then stores the result in `name`.

- **Python:** `x = 5`. No type needed.
- **C:** `int x = 5;`. The type comes first, and every statement ends with `;`.

`x = x + 1` is legal and common: read x, add 1, store it back. A **swap** needs a spare box: `t = a; a = b; b = t`. In Python, `y = x` for a **list** copies the *reference* (a second name), not the contents.
cards.intuition_full: Think of memory as a wall of lockers. Each variable name is a label stuck on one locker. An assignment is an order: 'open the locker on the left and put this value inside'. Before it stores anything, the computer finishes the whole right-hand side, which means reading the current contents of any lockers named there. That is why `x = x + 1` makes sense in code even though it is impossible as an equation: the right x is the old contents and the left x is the locker that receives the new value. Because each assignment overwrites, the order of lines matters. Swapping with `a = b; b = a` fails, since the first line destroys a before it was saved. Python adds one twist: a list is a big object stored elsewhere, and the variable holds a tag pointing to it. `q = p` copies the tag, so p and q share one list. A number is copied as a value, so `q = p` for numbers gives two independent boxes.

examples.setup:
Trace this Python program and give the final `x` and `y`.

```python
x = 5
y = x + 2
x = y * 2
y = x - y
```
steps: `x = 5`: box x holds 5.
`y = x + 2`: read x (5), compute 5 + 2 = 7, store 7 in y.
`x = y * 2`: read y (7), compute 7 × 2 = 14, store 14 in x. The old 5 is overwritten.
`y = x - y`: use the current values, 14 - 7 = 7, and store 7 in y. y holds 7 again.
Final boxes: x = 14, y = 7. Boxes hold values, not formulas: y did not change when x did.
examples.answer: x = 14 and y = 7.

steps: Start: a = 2, b = 3.
`a = a + b`: a becomes 2 + 3 = 5.
`b = a * b`: use the **new** a. b becomes 5 × 3 = 15.
`a = b - a`: use the new b and the new a. a becomes 15 - 5 = 10.
`printf` shows a then b: 10 and 15.
examples.answer: It prints `10 15`. The trap avoided: using the old a (2) in the later lines. Every line sees the values left by the lines above it.

examples.setup:
A list is not copied by `=`. What does this Python program print?

```python
p = [1, 2]
q = p
q.append(3)
print(p, len(q))
```
steps: `p = [1, 2]` creates a list and gives it the name p.
`q = p` copies the tag, not the list. p and q now name the **same** list.
`q.append(3)` changes that one list to `[1, 2, 3]`.
Printing p shows the same list: `[1, 2, 3]`. And `len(q)` is 3.
examples.answer: It prints `[1, 2, 3] 3`. For numbers `q = p` makes an independent copy, but for lists it makes a second name. Use `q = p.copy()` for a real copy.

cards.why: Every program is a list of assignments, so tracing a program means keeping a table of what each variable holds after each line. Misread one assignment and every later line is wrong. In GATE: output-tracing questions in C (Programming and Data Structures) and Python output questions in DA.
how: Draw each variable as a box and write its starting value.
Go line by line. On an assignment, work out the right side with the **current** values.
Overwrite the box on the left and cross out the old value.
After the last line, read off the values the question asks for.
cards.mistake: Reading `y = x` as an equation that stays true. It is a one-time copy: later changes to x never reach y. Another slip is using the old value of a variable after it was overwritten, as in `a = b; b = a`, which leaves both equal to the old b.
edge_cases: `x = x + 1` is valid code: the right x is the old value.
A local variable used before it has any value is an error in Python and holds a garbage value in C.
A swap without a spare box needs the add/subtract trick, or Python's `a, b = b, a`.
C integers have a fixed size, so a huge result can overflow. Python integers grow as needed.
connections: Used in: Programming and data structures. C output tracing and pointers (a pointer is a variable holding another box's address).
Used in: Python for DA. Aliasing of lists explains many surprising outputs.
Used in: Computer organization. A register is a variable stored in hardware, and a load or store instruction is an assignment.

check.q: After `a = 4`, `b = a * 2`, `a = a + 1`, what are a and b?
check.a: a = 5 and b = 8. b was worked out from the old a (4) and never changes afterwards.

check.q: Why does `a = b; b = a` not swap a and b?
check.a: The first line overwrites a, so the old a is lost. Then `b = a` copies that new value, which is just b again. Both end up equal to the old b.

check.q: In Python, `u = [7]`, `w = u`, `w.append(8)`. What is u?
check.a: `[7, 8]`. `w = u` made a second name for the same list.

cards.title: Integer division and modulo
cards.simple: Imagine you have 17 sweets and put them into packets of 5. You can fill 3 packets and 2 sweets are left over. The number of full packets is the quotient and the leftover sweets are the remainder. In code, `//` gives the packets (3) and `%` gives the leftovers (2). A clock uses the same idea: after 12 it starts again, so 14 o'clock is `14 % 12 = 2` o'clock. In exam words: `//` is integer (floor) division, `%` is modulo, and a = (a // b) × b + a % b. In C, plain `/` between two ints already does the integer division.
cards.idea: Division often leaves a leftover. Share 17 sweets into packets of 5: you fill **3** packets and **2** sweets remain. The number of full packets is the **quotient**, written `17 // 5` in Python, and the leftover is the **remainder**, written `17 % 5` (also called **modulo**). A remainder is always smaller than the divisor.
cards.definition:
For whole numbers a and b > 0:

$$a=(a\;//\;b)\times b+(a\bmod b),\qquad 0\le a\bmod b<b$$

`a // b` is how many whole b's fit in a. `a % b` is what is left over.

- **Python:** `/` gives a decimal (`17 / 5 = 3.4`), `//` gives the whole-number quotient.
- **C:** `/` between two `int`s already drops the fraction (`17 / 5 = 3`). `%` gives the remainder.
- **Negative numbers:** C and Python round differently (see the twist example).
cards.intuition_full: A remainder is what is left after you remove as many whole groups as you can. Two uses show up everywhere. First, **wrapping around**: a clock, the days of the week, or an array of size n all restart after a fixed count, and `x % n` always lands in the range 0 to n - 1. Second, **splitting a number into parts**: in base 10, `n % 10` is the last digit and `n // 10` is everything before it. In base 2 the same two operations, `n % 2` and `n // 2`, peel off bits. The identity a = (a // b) × b + a % b is your safety net: when you have a quotient and a remainder, multiply back and add to check. Finally, `n % 2 == 0` tests whether n is even, and `n % k == 0` tests whether k divides n exactly.

examples.setup: Share 17 sweets into packets of 5. Find `17 // 5` and `17 % 5`, then check the answer.
steps: 17 sweets, packets of 5. Each row of the picture is one packet.
Packet 1 takes sweets 1 to 5.
Packets 2 and 3 fill up too: 3 full packets, so `17 // 5 = 3`.
Sweets 16 and 17 are left. That is fewer than 5, so no fourth packet: `17 % 5 = 2`.
Check: 3 × 5 + 2 = 17, and the remainder 2 is smaller than 5.
Both operands are `int`, so `/` is integer division: the fraction is dropped.
`n / 100`: 739 ÷ 100 = 7.39, dropped to 7. That is the hundreds digit.
`n / 10 % 10`: `/` and `%` have the same priority and go left to right. 739 / 10 = 73, then 73 % 10 = 3. The tens digit.
`n % 10` = 739 - 73 × 10 = 9. The units digit.
examples.answer: It prints `7 3 9`. The trap avoided: reading `n / 100` as 7.39 (that needs a `double`).

examples.setup: Negative numbers. What are `-7 / 2` and `-7 % 2` in C99, and `-7 // 2` and `-7 % 2` in Python?
steps: The exact value of -7 ÷ 2 is -3.5.
C chops the fraction towards zero: quotient -3. Remainder = -7 - (-3 × 2) = -1.
Python rounds down, towards minus infinity: quotient -4. Remainder = -7 - (-4 × 2) = 1.
Check both with a = q × b + r: (-3) × 2 + (-1) = -7 and (-4) × 2 + 1 = -7.
examples.answer: C gives `-3` and `-1`. Python gives `-4` and `1`. The identity holds in both, but the quotient is rounded differently.

cards.why: `%` and `//` are how programs wrap around, split digits and test divisibility. Get them wrong and every digit-extraction loop, hash function and circular-buffer question goes wrong. In GATE: C output questions using `/` and `%` on ints, hash functions like `key % m`, and Python DA questions with `//`.
how: Check the types: two ints in C means integer division. In Python `/` always gives a decimal.
Find how many whole b's fit in a. That is the quotient.
Remainder = a - quotient × b.
With negative numbers, decide first which rounding the language uses.
Verify with a = q × b + r.
cards.mistake: Rounding the quotient up, or forgetting that C drops the fraction for ints. `7 / 2` is 3 in C and 3.5 in Python. A second slip is assuming `-7 % 2` is the same in both languages: C gives -1 and Python gives 1.
edge_cases: `a % b` with a < b is just a: `3 % 5 = 3`, and `3 // 5 = 0`.
`a % 1 = 0`, and `a % a = 0` for any positive a.
Dividing by zero crashes Python (`ZeroDivisionError`) and is undefined in C.
`x % 2` is 0 for even and 1 for odd, but for a negative odd number in C it gives -1.
connections: Used in: Programming and data structures. Hash functions (`key % m`), circular queues and array wrap-around.
Used in: Digital logic and COA. `n % 2` and `n // 2` are exactly the steps for converting a number to binary (see Binary basics).
Used in: Algorithms. Euclid's gcd repeats `a % b`.

check.q: What are `29 // 6` and `29 % 6`?
The loop variable i runs 0, 1, 2, ..., 12. Which values does `i % 5` take, in order?
In C, `printf("%.1f", 9 / 2 * 2.0);` prints what?
check.a: `9 / 2` is integer division = 4, then 4 × 2.0 = 8.0. So it prints 8.0, not 9.0.

cards.title: if / elif / else
cards.simple: An `if` is a fork in the road. The computer checks a yes/no question and takes the road that matches. With a chain like if / elif / else, it asks the questions in order and takes the first road whose answer is yes, then ignores the rest. It is like a grade chart: 'Is it 90 or above? No. 75 or above? No. 60 or above? Yes, grade C', and it never looks at the lower rows. In exam words: conditions use comparisons like `<` and `==`, joined by `and`, `or`, `not` (`&&`, `||`, `!` in C), and an `elif` chain runs only the first true branch.
cards.idea: An **if** statement lets a program choose. It tests a yes/no condition, such as `marks >= 60`, and runs its block only when the answer is yes. In an `if / elif / else` chain the tests run from the top and **only the first true branch runs**. Everything below it is skipped, even if it would also be true.
cards.definition:
```python
if cond1:
    ...   # runs if cond1 is true
elif cond2:
    ...   # only if cond1 was false and cond2 is true
else:
    ...   # only if all the conditions above were false
```

Conditions use `==` `!=` `<` `<=` `>` `>=`, joined by `and`, `or`, `not`.

- **C:** `&&`, `||`, `!` for the joiners, `{ }` for blocks, and `else if` instead of `elif`.
- In C, **0 is false and any other number is true**.
cards.intuition_full: A condition is an expression whose value is True or False. The `if` just checks it. An `elif` chain is **one decision with several outcomes**, so exactly one path (or none) runs. A separate `if` is a **new decision** that is checked no matter what happened before. Joining conditions has a rule GATE likes: `and` (`&&`) stops as soon as the left side is false, and `or` (`||`) stops as soon as the left side is true. This is called short-circuit evaluation, and it is what lets `x != 0 && 10 / x > 2` avoid a divide-by-zero. In C, truth is just an int: a comparison gives 1 or 0, and any non-zero number counts as true. That is why `if (x = 8)` compiles: the assignment's value is 8, which is true. Finally, in C an `else` always attaches to the nearest unmatched `if`, whatever the indentation suggests. Python uses indentation, so what you see is what runs.

examples.setup:
Trace this Python program.

```python
marks = 72
if marks >= 90: g = "A"
elif marks >= 75: g = "B"
elif marks >= 60: g = "C"
else: g = "D"
```
steps: `marks = 72`. Python now reads the chain from the top.
`marks >= 90`? 72 is below 90: **False**. Skip this branch.
`marks >= 75`? 72 is below 75: **False**. Skip this branch.
`marks >= 60`? 72 is at least 60: **True**. Run this branch: `g = "C"`.
The `else` is never tested. One branch ran and the chain is finished.
examples.answer: g is `"C"`.

steps: The `else` has no braces to say which `if` it belongs to. C attaches it to the **nearest** unmatched `if`, which is `if (b)`. The indentation is misleading.
Grouped properly: `if (a) { if (b) printf("X"); else printf("Y"); }`.
a = 0 is false, so the whole outer `if` is skipped, including the inner `if / else`.
`printf("Z")` is outside both and always runs.
examples.answer: It prints `Z`. The trap avoided: thinking the `else` belongs to `if (a)`, which would print `YZ`.

steps: `&&` evaluates the left side first: `x != 0` is false.
A false left side makes the whole `&&` false, so C **does not evaluate the right side**.
No division by zero happens. The condition is false, so `else` runs.
examples.answer: It prints `safe`. If the order were `10 / x > 2 && x != 0`, the program would divide by zero first.

cards.why: Almost every program makes choices, so tracing code means deciding which branch runs. One wrong branch makes the rest of the trace wrong. In GATE: C output questions with chains of if/else, dangling else, `=` versus `==`, and `&&` / `||` conditions that short-circuit.
how: Work out the condition with the current values of the variables.
In a chain, go top to bottom and stop at the first true test.
A separate `if` is always tested. Do not stop there.
Watch the boundaries: `<` versus `<=`, `>` versus `>=`.
In C, check the braces to see which `if` an `else` belongs to.
cards.mistake: Running every branch whose condition is true. In an `elif` chain only the first one runs. The other classic slip is `=` instead of `==` in a C condition: it assigns, then tests the assigned value.
edge_cases: In C, 0 is false and anything else is true, so `if (5)` always runs.
`and` / `&&` and `or` / `||` short-circuit, so the right side may never run.
`else` has no condition of its own and can only follow an `if` or `elif`.
Python's `elif` is written `else if` in C.
connections: Used in: Programming and data structures. Branches inside loops and recursion decide what a function returns.
Used in: Digital logic. An if/else is a 2-way multiplexer: a condition selects one of two values.
Used in: Algorithms. Search and sort are loops with an if inside.

check.q: `x = 10`. Which line prints: `if x > 5: print(1)`, then `elif x > 8: print(2)`, then `else: print(3)`?
check.a: Only `1`. The first test is true, so the chain stops and the `elif` is never reached.

check.q: What is `(7 > 3) and (2 > 5)`?
check.a: False. `and` needs both sides true, and 2 > 5 is false.

check.q: In C, does `if (-3)` run its block?
check.a: Yes. Any non-zero number is true, negative ones included.

Foundation, used in: ds.c, ds.python, ds.recursion, dl.comb.
cards.trap: Running every branch whose condition is true. In an `elif` chain only the first one runs. The other classic slip is `=` instead of `==` in a C condition: it assigns, then tests the assigned value.

cards.title: Loops and trace tables
cards.simple: A loop repeats the same few lines again and again. A `while` loop says 'keep going as long as this is true'. A `for` loop says 'do this once for each number in a list'. To follow a loop without getting lost, draw a small table. Each row is one lap of the loop and each column is a variable. Fill in the new values after every lap, and stop when the test fails. It is like a runner's log: lap number, distance so far, time so far. In exam words: this is a trace table, and the number of iterations is how many times the loop body runs.
cards.idea: A **loop** repeats a block of code. A `while` loop runs its body as long as a condition stays true. A `for` loop runs its body once for each value in a range. To predict the result, build a **trace table**: one column per variable, one row per pass, with the values written *after* each pass. Stop when the test is false.
cards.definition:
```python
while test:
    body

for i in range(start, stop, step):
    body
```
In C: `while (test) { body }` and `for (i = start; i < stop; i += step) { body }`.

`range(a, b, s)`, and its C twin `for (i = a; i < b; i += s)`, run $\lceil (b-a)/s \rceil$ times and never use `b` itself. A C `for` loop is a `while` loop with the setup, test and update written on one line.
cards.intuition_full: A loop is a machine with three parts: a setup (before the first pass), a test (checked before every pass) and an update (changes a variable so that the test finally fails). The trace table is a log of that machine. Always write a row for the state *before* the loop, so you have the starting values. Each pass is then: check the test with the current values; if it is true, run the body line by line and write a new row; if it is false, stop. For simple counting loops there is a shortcut. `for (i = 2; i <= 30; i += 4)` visits 2, 6, 10, ..., 30, which is (30 - 2) / 4 + 1 = 8 values, with the + 1 because both ends count. With `<` instead of `<=`, the end value is left out. If the update goes the wrong way (such as `i--` when counting up), the loop never ends. If the test is false at the start, the body runs zero times.

examples.setup:
Trace this Python loop with a table and find `total` at the end.

```python
n = 1
total = 0
while n < 20:
    total += n
    n *= 2
```
steps: Before the loop: n = 1 and total = 0. This is row 0 of the table.
Pass 1: test 1 < 20 is True. total = 0 + 1 = 1, then n = 1 × 2 = 2.
Pass 5: 16 < 20 is still True. total = 15 + 16 = 31, n = 32.
Test 32 < 20 is False, so the loop ends after 5 passes.
examples.answer: `total` is 31 after 5 passes, and n ends at 32.

steps: i starts at 10 and drops by 3: the values tested are 10, 7, 4, 1, -2.
10, 7, 4 and 1 are all > 0, so the body runs 4 times: count = 4.
After the body for i = 1, the update makes i = -2.
`-2 > 0` is false, so the loop ends with i = -2. The loop variable keeps the value that ended the loop.
`printf` shows count and i.
examples.answer: It prints `4 -2`. The trap avoided: printing i = 1, its last value inside the loop, instead of the value that made the test fail.

examples.setup: Compare the loop variable after the loop in each language. C: `for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) {}`. Python: `for i in range(3): pass`. What is i afterwards in each?
steps: C runs the update after every pass, including the last one, so i goes 0, 1, 2, 3. The test `3 < 3` fails.
In C, i is therefore **3** after the loop.
Python's `for` just takes the next value from `range(3)`: 0, 1, 2. Nothing is updated after the last value.
In Python, i is **2** after the loop.
examples.answer: C leaves i = 3 and Python leaves i = 2. If the range is empty, such as `range(0)`, Python never assigns i at all.

cards.why: Loops are where programs do their work, and where most of the running time goes. A trace table is the method to use in the exam, and counting iterations is the first step towards time complexity. In GATE: C output tracing with for and while loops, counting how often a statement runs, and Python loops over ranges in DA questions.
how: Write every variable and its starting value (row 0).
Check the test with the current values. False means stop.
Run the body line by line, using the latest values.
Write a new row after each pass and repeat.
For a plain counting loop, use $\lceil (b-a)/s \rceil$ and test it on the first and last values.
cards.mistake: Off-by-one errors: treating `<` as `<=`, counting the end value of `range`, or reporting the last value of i inside the loop instead of the value that ended it. These slips happen when you skip the trace table and do it in your head.
edge_cases: A test that is false at the start: the body runs 0 times (`range(5, 5)`, `range(10, 0)`).
A loop whose update never makes the test false runs forever.
`range(10, 0, -3)` counts down: 10, 7, 4, 1.
`while` and `for` are interchangeable: a `for` is a `while` with setup, test and update on one line.
connections: Used in: Algorithms. Counting iterations is the first step in finding time complexity.
Used in: Programming and data structures. Every array and linked-list traversal is a loop.
Used in: Digital logic. A sequential circuit steps through states, a loop built in hardware.

check.q: How many times does `for i in range(2, 11, 3)` run?
check.a: i = 2, 5, 8. The next value, 11, is not below 11. So 3 times.

check.q: Python: `n = 100`, then `while n > 10: n = n // 3`. How many passes?
check.a: n goes 100 → 33 → 11 → 3. The tests 100 > 10, 33 > 10 and 11 > 10 pass; 3 > 10 fails. So 3 passes.

check.q: In C, after `for (i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {}`, what is i?
check.a: 5. The update runs after the last pass, and then `5 <= 4` fails.

cards.title: Arrays and lists
cards.simple: An array (called a list in Python) is a row of numbered lockers. Each locker holds one value and has a number on its door. The numbering starts at 0, not 1, so a row of 6 lockers is numbered 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. To get the value in a locker you say its number: `a[3]` means 'open locker 3'. Asking for locker 6 in that row fails, because it does not exist. In exam words: an index is the position counted from 0, the last index is the length minus 1, and `a[i]` reads the element at index i. Python also lets you count from the end with negative numbers.
cards.idea: An **array** (a **list** in Python) is a row of cells that share one name and are told apart by a number, the **index**. Indices start at **0**. A row of n cells has indices 0 to n - 1, and `a[i]` is the value in cell i. A loop over the indices lets you process every cell with the same few lines.
cards.definition:
```python
a = [12, 7, 30, 5, 19, 8]          # Python list
```
```c
int a[6] = {12, 7, 30, 5, 19, 8};  /* C array */
```
`a[i]` reads or writes cell i. Valid indices are $0, 1, \dots, n-1$.

- **Python:** `len(a)` is the number of cells. `a[-1]` is the last cell (negative indices count from the end). `a[i:j]` is a slice from i up to, but not including, j.
- **C:** the size is fixed when the array is created, and there is **no bounds check**: `a[6]` reads whatever sits in memory after the array.
cards.intuition_full: Memory is a long street of numbered houses, and an array reserves a block of n houses in a row. The index says how many houses to walk from the first one. That is why the first house is index 0 (distance zero) and the last is n - 1, not n. The computer does exactly this: the address of `a[i]` is the start address plus i times the size of one element. Loops and arrays go together: `for i in range(len(a))` visits every cell once. Three patterns cover most questions: a running total (`s += a[i]`), the best so far (`m = a[0]`, then replace m when you find a bigger a[i]), and writing results into another array. A Python list can grow with `append`, but a C array cannot.

examples.setup: Given `a = [12, 7, 30, 5, 19, 8]`, find `a[0]`, `a[3]`, the last element and `a[1] + a[4]`. What happens with `a[6]`?
steps: Six cells, with indices 0 to 5 written under them.
`a[0]` is the first cell: 12.
`a[3]` is three cells after the start: 5.
The last cell has index `len(a) - 1 = 5`: `a[5]` is 8.
`a[6]` does not exist. Python raises an `IndexError`. C silently reads whatever follows the array.
examples.answer: `a[0] = 12`, `a[3] = 5`, the last element is 8, `a[1] + a[4] = 26`, and `a[6]` is out of range.

examples.setup:
What does this Python program print?

```python
a = [12, 7, 30, 5, 19, 8]
m = a[0]
for i in range(1, len(a)):
    if a[i] > m:
        m = a[i]
print(m, i)
```
steps: m starts as a[0] = 12.
`range(1, 6)` ends at 5, so Python leaves i = 5 after the loop.
`print(m, i)` shows the maximum and the last i.
examples.answer: It prints `30 5`. The trap avoided: printing the index of the maximum (2) when the code prints the loop variable i.

examples.setup: Negative indices and slices on the same list: what are `a[-1]`, `a[-6]`, `a[2:4]` and `a[4:10]`?
steps: `a[-1]` counts from the end: the last element, 8.
`a[-6]` is the sixth from the end, which is the first element: 12.
`a[2:4]` takes indices 2 and 3 (not 4): `[30, 5]`.
`a[4:10]` runs past the end, but a slice never raises an error: it stops at the end and gives `[19, 8]`. A single `a[10]` would raise an `IndexError`.

cards.why: Arrays hold the data nearly every algorithm works on, and index mistakes are the commonest way to get a wrong trace. In GATE: C and Python output questions that read, write and loop over arrays, plus the index work inside sorting, searching and DP chapters.
how: Write the indices under the array, starting at 0.
To read `a[i]`, find the cell with index i. Never count from 1.
For a loop over `range(len(a))`, trace i and the cell it reads on each pass.
Track running values (total, best so far) in a trace table.
Check that the last index is n - 1 before you read or write.
cards.mistake: Counting positions from 1. `a[3]` is the **fourth** element. A second slip is assuming the last index is n, which gives an `IndexError` in Python and silent garbage (or a crash) in C.
edge_cases: An empty list has no `a[0]`: it raises `IndexError`.
C does not check bounds: `a[6]` on a 6-element array is undefined behaviour.
Python slices never raise: `a[4:10]` just stops at the end.
A string behaves like a list of characters: `'hello'[1]` is `'e'`.
connections: Used in: Programming and data structures (Arrays, Stacks, Queues). All of them are built on index arithmetic.
Used in: Algorithms. Searching, sorting and DP tables all index into arrays.
Used in: Python for DA. NumPy arrays and pandas columns use the same 0-based indexing.

check.a: `b[2] = 15` (the third element) and `b[-2] = 15` (second from the end). Same cell here.

check.a: It raises `IndexError`: the last valid index is `len(a) - 1`.

cards.title: Functions and parameters
cards.simple: A function is a small machine with a name. You give it some inputs (called parameters when they sit in the function's brackets), it does its job, and it hands back one answer with `return`. Think of a photocopier: you give the helper a COPY of your homework and they scribble on it. Your original stays clean. So if a function changes its input number, the number in the line that called it does not change. The only thing that comes back is the answer you `return`. In exam words: arguments are passed by value, local variables disappear when the function ends, and `return` gives the value of the call.
cards.idea: A **function** packages some code under a name so you can reuse it. When you call `f(x)`, the value of `x` is **copied** into the function's own variable, the **parameter**. The function works on its copy, so the caller's variable is unchanged. The only thing that comes back is the value of the `return` statement.
cards.definition:
```python
def f(n):          # n is the parameter
    n = n * 2      # changes f's own n
    return n + 1   # sends a value back

y = f(5)           # 5 is the argument
```
```c
int f(int n) { n = n * 2; return n + 1; }
```
A call is an **expression**: it is replaced by its returned value. A function's variables are **local**: they exist only during the call. A Python function that ends without `return` gives back `None`. A **list** that is passed in is shared, so `append` inside the function is visible outside.
cards.intuition_full: Think of a call as a short trip into a new room. The room has its own empty lockers (the parameters and local variables). On entry, the values you pass are copied into those lockers. Inside, the function can do whatever it wants to its own lockers, and the caller's lockers are out of reach. On exit the room is cleared, and only the returned value is carried back to where the call was. This is exactly how the call stack works, which is why recursion needs it. When one call sits inside another, such as `f(f(1, 2), 3)`, work from the inside out: replace the inner call with its returned value, then evaluate the outer call. A caution: in Python, numbers, strings and tuples cannot be changed by the callee, but a list or dict is shared, so `lst.append(x)` shows through. In C, passing an array or a pointer likewise lets the function change the caller's data.

examples.setup:
Trace this Python program and give `x` and `y`.

```python
def f(n):
    n = n * 2
    return n + 1

x = 5
y = f(x)
```
steps: `x = 5`: main's box x holds 5.
`y = f(x)` calls f. The value 5 is copied into f's own box n.
`n = n * 2` changes f's n to 10. main's x is still 5.
`return n + 1` sends back 10 + 1 = 11. f's box n then disappears.
y receives 11.
Final: x = 5 (unchanged) and y = 11.
examples.answer: x is 5 and y is 11.

steps: Work inside out: the inner call is `f(1, 2)`.
Inner: a = 1, b = 2, so it returns 1 × 10 + 2 = 12.
The outer call becomes `f(12, 3)`.
Outer: a = 12, b = 3, so it returns 12 × 10 + 3 = 123.
`printf` prints 123.
examples.answer: It prints `123`. The trap avoided: swapping the argument order, which would give f(3, 12) = 42.

examples.setup:
A function with no `return`. What does this Python program print?

```python
def add_one(x):
    x = x + 1

r = add_one(4)
print(r)
```
steps: `add_one(4)` copies 4 into x and sets x to 5 inside the function.
There is no `return`, so the function ends and gives back `None`.
r receives `None`. The 5 was thrown away with the function's local x.
examples.answer: It prints `None`. A function must `return` its answer. Changing a local variable does not send it back.

cards.why: Functions are how programs are structured, and every recursion and call-stack question depends on knowing what is copied and what is returned. In GATE: C output tracing with function calls, nested calls and the by-value rule, and in Python the shared-list behaviour.
how: Work inside out: evaluate the innermost call first.
Copy each argument into its parameter, in order.
Run the body with the parameters as local variables.
The call's value is the returned value. Put it where the call was.
The caller's own variables change only if you return and assign, or share a list or pointer.
cards.mistake: Expecting a function to change the caller's number. `a = a + b` inside a function changes only the function's copy. The other slip is forgetting that a list or array is shared, so changes made inside show up outside.
edge_cases: A Python function without `return` gives `None`.
A parameter and a caller's variable may share a name. They are still different boxes.
Argument order matters: `f(1, 2)` and `f(2, 1)` are different calls.
A function can call itself (recursion), with one fresh set of locals per call.
connections: Used in: Programming and data structures (Recursion). Each call gets its own copy of the parameters on the call stack.
Used in: Programming and data structures (C pointers). A pointer parameter lets a function change the caller's variable.
Used in: Compiler design. Activation records implement exactly this copy-in, return-out scheme.

check.q: `def g(x): return x * x`. What is `g(3) + g(2)`?
If a function changes its parameter `n` (a number), does the caller's variable change?
check.a: No. `n` is a copy, and the caller's box is untouched.

cards.title: Nested loops
cards.simple: A loop inside a loop is like the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock. The hour hand (the outer loop) moves one step, and for each hour step the minute hand (the inner loop) goes all the way round. If the hour hand takes 2 steps and the minute hand does 5 steps each time, the minute hand moves 2 × 5 = 10 times in total. So to count how often the inner line runs, multiply the loop counts. If the inner loop gets shorter each time, add the counts instead: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1. In exam words: the body of nested loops runs (outer count) × (inner count) times when the inner range does not depend on the outer variable.
cards.idea: A **nested loop** is a loop inside another loop. For each pass of the outer loop, the inner loop runs completely from its start. If the inner loop always has the same length, the body runs **outer × inner** times. Picture a grid: each row is one outer pass and each cell is one inner pass.
cards.definition:
```python
for i in range(R):        # R outer passes
    for j in range(C):    # C inner passes for every i
        body              # runs R × C times
```
When the inner range depends on i, count the inner passes for each i and **add** them.

- Outer `i` from 0 to n-1 with inner `for j in range(i)`: $0+1+\dots+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ passes in total.
- Outer `i` from 1 to n with inner `j` from 1 to i: $1+2+\dots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ passes in total.
cards.intuition_full: Counting loop runs is counting cells in a picture. Draw one row for each value of the outer variable, and in that row draw one cell for each value the inner variable takes. If every row is the same length the picture is a rectangle, and its area is rows × columns. If the row length grows or shrinks with i, the picture is a triangle, and its area is the sum of the row lengths. If the inner step doubles (`j *= 2`), each row has about $\log_2 n$ cells, so the total is about $n\log_2 n$. Two loops one after the other, not nested, **add**: 5 passes then 7 passes make 12 runs, not 35. The same picture is how you read time complexity: an n by n rectangle of cells is $n^2$ steps. And it is how you trace: the inner variable starts again from its first value every time the outer loop moves one step.

steps: The outer loop gives i = 0, 1. For each i, the inner loop gives j = 0 to 4. Each grid cell is one `print`.
i = 0, j = 0: the first print, `0 0`. One so far.
The inner loop finishes all of j = 0 to 4 before i changes. Row i = 0 is full: 5 prints.
i = 1: the inner loop restarts at j = 0 and runs 5 more times. Now 10 prints.
Total = outer count × inner count = 2 × 5 = 10.
The inner loop runs i times for each i (j goes from 1 to i).
Formula check: n(n + 1)/2 = 6 × 7 / 2 = 21.
examples.answer: `count` is 21. The trap avoided: multiplying 6 × 6 = 36, which is right only when the inner loop always runs n times.

cards.mistake: Multiplying when the inner range changes (n × n instead of n(n + 1)/2), or adding when the loops are nested. Also off-by-one slips at the start and end values of the inner loop.
edge_cases: If the outer loop runs 0 times, the inner loop never starts.
`for j in range(i)` gives 0 passes when i = 0, so a triangle can start with an empty row.
A `break` in the inner loop leaves only the inner loop, not the outer one.
A variable set before the inner loop (like a running total) keeps its value across rows.

cards.what_full:
A **nested loop** is a loop inside another loop. For each pass of the outer loop, the inner loop runs completely from its start. If the inner loop always has the same length, the body runs **outer × inner** times. Picture a grid: each row is one outer pass and each cell is one inner pass.

```python
for i in range(R):        # R outer passes
    for j in range(C):    # C inner passes for every i
        body              # runs R × C times
```
When the inner range depends on i, count the inner passes for each i and **add** them.

- Outer `i` from 0 to n-1 with inner `for j in range(i)`: $0+1+\dots+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ passes in total.
- Outer `i` from 1 to n with inner `j` from 1 to i: $1+2+\dots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ passes in total.

**Worked example.** How many times does `print` run, and in what order?

```python
for i in range(2):
    for j in range(5):
        print(i, j)
```

1. The outer loop gives i = 0, 1. For each i, the inner loop gives j = 0 to 4. Each grid cell is one `print`.
2. i = 0, j = 0: the first print, `0 0`. One so far.
3. The inner loop finishes all of j = 0 to 4 before i changes. Row i = 0 is full: 5 prints.
4. i = 1: the inner loop restarts at j = 0 and runs 5 more times. Now 10 prints.
5. Total = outer count × inner count = 2 × 5 = 10.

**Answer:** `print` runs 10 times, in the order (0,0) (0,1) ... (0,4) (1,0) ... (1,4).

steps.caption: x = 5 puts the number 5 into box x. The box now exists and holds 5.
y = x + 2: read x (5), work out 5 + 2 = 7, store 7 in box y.
x = y * 2: read y (7), work out 14, store it in x. The old 5 is overwritten and gone.
y = x - y: use the current values, 14 - 7 = 7. Box y gets 7 again.
Final: x = 14 and y = 7. Boxes hold values, not formulas, so y did not follow x.
We have 17 sweets and packets that hold 5. Each row of the grid is one packet.
Packet 1 takes sweets 1 to 5.
Packets 2 and 3 fill up as well: 3 full packets. That count is 17 // 5 = 3.
Sweets 16 and 17 are left. That is fewer than 5, so there is no fourth packet. Left over: 17 % 5 = 2.
Check: 3 full packets of 5 plus 2 left over rebuilds the 17, and 2 is less than 5.

steps.caption: marks is 72. Python reads the chain from the top, one test at a time.
marks >= 90? 72 is below 90: False. Skip this branch.
marks >= 75? 72 is below 75: False. Skip this branch too.
marks >= 60? 72 is at least 60: True. Run this branch: g = "C".

scenes.title: A while loop and its trace table

steps.caption: Before the loop: n = 1 and total = 0. Write them as row 0 of the table.
Pass 1: test 1 < 20 is True. total = 0 + 1 = 1, then n = 1 * 2 = 2.
Pass 5: 16 < 20 is still True. total = 15 + 16 = 31, n = 32.
Test 32 < 20 is False, so the loop ends after 5 passes. total = 31.
Six cells. The small number under each cell is its index, and it starts at 0.
a[0] is the first cell: 12.
a[3] is three cells after the start. It holds 5.
The last cell has index len(a) - 1 = 6 - 1 = 5. It holds 8.
a[6] does not exist. Python raises an IndexError. C reads whatever sits after the array.

scenes.title: A call copies the value into the function

steps.caption: x = 5: the box x in main holds 5.
y = f(x) calls f. The value 5 is copied into f's own new box n.
n = n * 2 changes f's n to 10. main's x is still 5.
return n + 1 sends back 10 + 1 = 11. Then f's box n disappears.
The returned 11 is stored in y. The whole f room is gone.
Final: x = 5 (unchanged) and y = 11.
